title: Surface Integrals
lead: A surface integral is a line integral one dimension up: it integrates over a surface described by two parameters. This section parameterizes cylinders, cones, spheres and graphs, finds surface area from the tangent vectors of a parameterization, integrates scalar functions over surfaces, chooses an orientation, and defines the flux of a vector field across a surface, with mass flow and heat flow.
objectives: Find the parametric representations of a cylinder, a cone, and a sphere.
Describe the surface integral of a scalar-valued function over a parametric surface.
Use a surface integral to calculate the area of a given surface.
Explain the meaning of an oriented surface, giving an example.
Describe the surface integral of a vector field.
Use surface integrals to solve applied problems.
summary_html:
• Surfaces can be parameterized, just as curves can be parameterized. In general, surfaces must be parameterized with two parameters.
  • Surfaces can sometimes be oriented, just as curves can be oriented. Some surfaces, such as a Möbius strip, cannot be oriented.
  • A surface integral is like a line integral in one higher dimension. The domain of integration of a surface integral is a surface in a plane or space, rather than a curve in a plane or space.
  • The integrand of a surface integral can be a scalar function or a vector field. To calculate a surface integral with an integrand that is a function, use Equation 16.19. To calculate a surface integral with an integrand that is a vector field, use Equation 16.20.
  • If S is a surface, then the area of S is $\int \int_{S}dS .$

For the following exercises, determine whether the statements are true or false.

If surface S is given by $\{(x,y,z):0\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1,z=10\},$ then $\iint_{S}f(x,y,z) dS=\int_0^{1}\int_0^{1}f(x,y,10) dxdy.$

For the following exercises, determine whether the statements are true or false.

If surface S is given by $\{(x,y,z):0\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1,z=x\},$ then $\iint_{S}f(x,y,z) dS=\int_0^{1}\int_0^{1}f(x,y,x) dxdy.$

answer.solution: False. Parameterize $S$ by $\textbf{r}(x,y)=\langle x,y,x\rangle,$ $0\le x\le 1,$ $0\le y\le 1.$ Then $\textbf{t}_{x}=\langle 1,0,1\rangle$ and $\textbf{t}_{y}=\langle 0,1,0\rangle,$ so $\textbf{t}_{x}\times\textbf{t}_{y}=\langle -1,0,1\rangle$ and $\|\textbf{t}_{x}\times\textbf{t}_{y}\|=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence $\iint_{S}f\,dS=\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}f(x,y,x)\,dx\,dy,$ which differs from the stated integral by the factor $\sqrt{2}$ whenever that integral is not zero.

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, determine whether the statements are true or false.

Surface $\textbf{r}=\langle v\;\cos u,v\;\sin u,v^{2}\rangle ,\;\text{for}\;0\le u\le \pi ,0\le v\le 2,$ is the same as surface $\textbf{r}=\langle \sqrt{v}\;\cos 2u,\sqrt{v}\;\sin 2u,v\rangle ,$ for $0\le u\le \frac{\pi}{2},0\le v\le 4.$

For the following exercises, determine whether the statements are true or false.

Given the standard parameterization of a sphere, normal vectors ${\text{t}}_u^{}\;\times \;{\text{t}}_{v}$ are outward normal vectors.

answer.solution: True, when $u=\varphi$ and $v=\theta$ in the standard parameterization $\textbf{r}(\varphi,\theta)=\langle \rho\cos\theta\sin\varphi,\rho\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\rho\cos\varphi\rangle:$ as computed for the sphere’s surface area, $\textbf{t}_{\varphi}\times\textbf{t}_{\theta}=\rho^{2}\sin\varphi\,\langle \cos\theta\sin\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\varphi\rangle=\rho\sin\varphi\,\textbf{r},$ a nonnegative multiple of the position vector, which points outward. Taking the parameters in the other order reverses the cross product and gives the inward normals.

footnotes.html: The inner integral’s upper limit is printed $\pi;$ the angle runs over $0\le\theta\le 2\pi,$ which gives the factor $2\pi$ on the next line.
The book prints “scalar line integral”; the definition extended here is that of the scalar surface integral.

In this part the integrand is printed as $1$ (“$\iint_{S_{2}}dS$”) and as $z$ (“$\iint_{S_{2}}z\,dS$”); it is $z^{2}$ throughout, as the computation uses. $\mathbf{t}_{\theta}$’s second component is printed $u\cos\theta\sin\varphi$ for $2\cos\theta\sin\varphi,$ and the last bracket $[\frac{1}{3}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{8}]$ for $[\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{24}]=\frac{7}{24},$ which gives $\frac{28\pi}{3}.$

The tangent vector $\mathbf{t}_{y}$ is printed $\langle 1,0,2\rangle;$ it is $\langle 0,1,2\rangle,$ with the same cross product $\langle -1,-2,1\rangle.$ The link names Equation 16.5, the scalar line integral; the computation uses Equation 16.19, the scalar surface integral.
The rate of flow per unit area is printed $\rho\mathbf{N};$ it is $\rho\mathbf{v},$ whose component along $\mathbf{N}$ the next sentences use.
The book prints this reference as “[link]”; it points to the unnumbered computation before Equation 16.21.
The caption’s second bound is printed $0\le x\lt 2\pi;$ it is $0\le\theta\lt 2\pi.$

assumes.text: The piece $S_{ij}$ is approximated by the parallelogram in the tangent plane at $P_{ij}$ spanned by $\Delta u\,\kvectu(P_{ij})$ and $\Delta v\,\kvectv(P_{ij})$.
The area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $\kvecu$ and $\kvecv$ is $\|\kvecu\times\kvecv\|$.

steps.cap: $\Delta u$ and $\Delta v$ are positive, so they come out of the magnitude as they are.

derivations.what: the scalar surface integral as a double integral
derivations.source: Calculus, 16.6 Surface Integrals, Surface Integral of a Scalar-Valued Function

assumes.text: Point $P_{ij}$ corresponds to the point $(u_{i},v_{j})$ of the parameter domain $\kD$: $P_{ij}=\kvecr(u_{i},v_{j})$.
The limit of a double Riemann sum $\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}g(u_{i},v_{j})\Delta u\Delta v$ over $\kD$ is the double integral $\iint_{D}g(u,v)dA$.

steps.cap: The approximation becomes arbitrarily close as $m$ and $n$ go to infinity, and the limit of the double Riemann sum is a double integral over $\kD.$
